prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 500 words of the Boston molasses flood of 1919. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
At about half past noon on 15 January 1919, a steel tank at the Purity Distilling Company's plant on Commercial Street in Boston's North End burst open. The tank was 50 feet high and 90 feet across, and it held roughly 2.3 million gallons of molasses, which weighed around 13,000 tons. The company stored the molasses there before turning it into industrial alcohol, a large share of which went to make munitions for the First World War.

The tank had been built in 1915 by the United States Industrial Alcohol Company, the parent of Purity Distilling, and it was put up quickly. It was never tested by filling it with water, and the people who built it did not have an engineer review the design. The steel was thinner than it should have been for the load. From the start the tank leaked, and the leaks were bad enough that neighbours collected the molasses that ran down its sides. Rather than repair the seams, the company painted the tank brown so the stains would not show. A fresh delivery had arrived only the day before, and the weather had turned unusually warm after a cold snap, which may have added to the strain on the tank.

Witnesses described a low rumble and a sound like machine-gun fire, which was the rivets popping out of the steel. The tank failed, and a wave of molasses estimated at 25 feet high at its front moved out across the neighbourhood at about 35 miles an hour. It knocked a section of the Boston Elevated Railway's structure off its supports and pushed a firehouse off its foundation. Houses were crushed, and a number of people were caught in the flow. The molasses was cold, which made it thicker than usual, and that made it harder for anyone caught in it to move.

Twenty-one people died and about 150 were injured. Those killed included children who had been playing nearby and firemen from the damaged station. Rescuers waded in and found it hard to reach victims who were stuck. Soldiers and sailors from nearby ships and the Charlestown Navy Yard arrived to help, as did Red Cross workers and local people. It took days to find all the bodies, and the harbour ran brown with molasses for months. The smell persisted in the area for years, and some residents say it can still be noticed on hot days, though that is a local belief and not something that has been measured.

The lawsuit that followed was one of the first major class actions in Massachusetts. The company argued that anarchists had blown up the tank, a claim that fitted the fears of the period. A court-appointed auditor, Hugh Ogden, heard testimony for several years, and he concluded that the tank had not been built to a safe standard. The company was found liable in 1925 and paid out about 628,000 dollars in settlements, with families of the dead receiving around 7,000 dollars each. The case is often credited with prompting stricter rules on construction, requiring engineers to sign off on plans, which in time became standard practice.
